\[
e_n^*:=\max_{\{x,y\}\in E_{n}} |x-y|,
\qquad
E_{n}:=\bigl\{\{x,y\}\in E:\ x\in V\cap B_n\bigr\},
\]
as well as the exceedance count $F(n,r)$ from
\begin{align}
F(n,r)
&:= \sum_{x\in V\cap B_n}\sum_{y\in V\cap B_n^c}
\mathbf{1}_{\{|x-y|>r_n,\, x\leftrightarrow y\}}
+ \frac12\sum_{x\in V\cap B_n}\sum_{y\in V\cap B_n}
\mathbf{1}_{\{|x-y|>r_n,\, x\leftrightarrow y\}},
\label{eq:Fnr-intro}
\end{align}
Assume that the weight distribution satisfies $\mathbb{P}(W>w)=w^{-\beta}$ for $w\ge 1$, with tail index $\beta>0$, and that the
finite-degree condition
\begin{equation}\label{eq:finite-degree-cond-intro}
\min\{\alpha,\alpha\beta\}>d.
\end{equation}
holds.

\smallskip
For $r>0$ set $r_n=c_n r$ and define
\[
\theta=
\begin{cases}
\alpha\beta-d, & 0<\beta<1,\\
\alpha-d, & \beta\ge 1.
\end{cases}
\]
Then, in each of the regimes \textup{(a)}--\textup{(c)} below, with the corresponding choice of $c_n$, we have
\begin{equation*}\label{eq:pois-frechet-unified}
F(n,r)\ \xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{d}\ \mathrm{Poisson}\!\bigl(r^{-\theta}\bigr),
\qquad
\mathbb{P}\!\left(c_n^{-1}e_n^*\le r\right)\ \longrightarrow\ \exp\!\bigl(-r^{-\theta}\bigr),
\qquad r>0,
\end{equation*}
that is, $c_n^{-1}e_n^*$ converges in distribution to a Fr\'echet random variable with parameter $\theta$.

\smallskip
\noindent\textup{(a) {Infinite-mean regime} $(0<\beta<1)$.}
Assume $\alpha\beta\in(d,2d]$ and set
\[
c_n=C_1\,n^{\frac{d}{\alpha\beta-d}}(\log n)^{\frac{1}{\alpha\beta-d}}.
\]

\smallskip
\noindent\textup{(b) {Borderline regime} $(\beta=1)$.}
Assume $\alpha\in(d,2d]$ and set
\[
c_n=C_2\,n^{\frac{d}{\alpha-d}}(\log n)^{\frac{2}{\alpha-d}}.
\]

\smallskip
\noindent\textup{(c) {Finite-mean regime} $(\beta>1)$.}
Assume $\alpha\in(d,2d)$ and set
\[
c_n=C_3\,n^{\frac{d}{\alpha-d}}.
\]
Here $C_1, C_2, C_3\in(0,\infty)$ denote explicit constants independent of $n$. Specifically, we use the following corollary.

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:cn-choice}
Let $\theta:=\alpha\beta-d$ if $0<\beta<1$ and $\theta:=\alpha-d$ if $\beta\ge 1$. Define $c_n$ by
\[
c_n:=
\begin{cases}
\Bigl(2^d\omega_d\,\Gamma(1-\beta)\lambda^\beta\,\beta\,\dfrac{d}{\alpha\beta-d}\cdot \dfrac{\alpha d}{\theta}\Bigr)^{1/\theta}
\,n^{d/\theta}(\log n)^{1/\theta},
& 0<\beta<1,\\[2mm]
\Bigl(2^d\omega_d\,\dfrac12\lambda\,\dfrac{d}{\alpha-d}\cdot \dfrac{\alpha^2 d^2}{\theta^2}\Bigr)^{1/\theta}
\,n^{d/\theta}(\log n)^{2/\theta},
& \beta=1,\\[2mm]
\Bigl(2^d\omega_d\,\lambda\,\dfrac{\beta^2}{(\beta-1)^2}\,\dfrac{d}{\alpha-d}\Bigr)^{1/\theta}
\,n^{d/\theta},
& \beta>1,
\end{cases}
\]
and set $r_n=c_n r$ for fixed $r>0$. Then
\[
I_1 \sim r^{-\theta},
\qquad n\to\infty.
\]
\end{corollary}

mcq.question:
Consider the continuum random graph on a homogeneous Poisson point process V on \(\mathbb{R}^d\) with unit intensity, with i.i.d. weights \(\{W_x\}\) satisfying \(\mathbb{P}(W>w)=w^{-\beta}\) for \(w\ge 1\) (\(\beta>0\)). Edges between distinct points \(x,y\in V\) are present independently with probability
\[
 p_{xy}=1-\exp\Bigl\{-\lambda\,\frac{W_xW_y}{|x-y|^\alpha}\Bigr\},\qquad \lambda>0,\ \alpha>0.
\]
For \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), let \(B_n=[-n,n]^d\) and define
\[
E_n:=\bigl\{\{x,y\}\in E:\ x\in V\cap B_n\bigr\},\qquad e_n^*:=\max_{\{x,y\}\in E_n}|x-y|,
\]
and for \(r>0\) set \(r_n=c_n r\) and define the exceedance count
\[
F(n,r):= \sum_{x\in V\cap B_n}\sum_{y\in V\cap B_n^c}
\mathbf{1}_{\{|x-y|>r_n,\, x\leftrightarrow y\}}
+ \frac12\sum_{x\in V\cap B_n}\sum_{y\in V\cap B_n}
\mathbf{1}_{\{|x-y|>r_n,\, x\leftrightarrow y\}}.
\]
Assume the finite-degree condition \(\min\{\alpha,\alpha\beta\}>d\). Define
\[
\theta=\begin{cases}
\alpha\beta-d,&0<\beta<1,\\
\alpha-d,&\beta\ge 1.
\end{cases}
\]
In each of the following regimes, with the stated assumptions and choice of \(c_n\): (a) \(0<\beta<1\) and \(\alpha\beta\in(d,2d]\) with \(c_n=C_1 n^{\frac{d}{\alpha\beta-d}}(\log n)^{\frac{1}{\alpha\beta-d}}\); (b) \(\beta=1\) and \(\alpha\in(d,2d]\) with \(c_n=C_2 n^{\frac{d}{\alpha-d}}(\log n)^{\frac{2}{\alpha-d}}\); (c) \(\beta>1\) and \(\alpha\in(d,2d)\) with \(c_n=C_3 n^{\frac{d}{\alpha-d}}\), where \(C_1,C_2,C_3\in(0,\infty)\) are constants independent of \(n\). As \(n\to\infty\) (for fixed \(r>0\)), what is the strongest limiting conclusion about \(F(n,r)\) and \(e_n^*\)?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text:
In each regime (a)–(c), for every fixed r>0 (with r_n=c_n r and θ as defined),
\[
F(n,r)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{d}\mathrm{Poisson}(r^{-\theta}),
\]
and
\[
\mathbb{P}(c_n^{-1}e_n^*\le r)\longrightarrow \exp(-r^{-\theta})\quad (r>0),
\]
i.e. \(c_n^{-1}e_n^*\) converges in distribution to a Fr\'echet random variable with distribution function \(\exp(-r^{-\theta})\) on \((0,\infty)\).

choices.label: B
choices.text:
In each regime (a)–(c), for every fixed $r>0$ (with $r_n=c_n r$ and $\theta$ as defined),
\[
F(n,r)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{d}\mathrm{Poisson}\bigl(r^{-\theta}\bigr),
\]
but the maximum edge length has the degenerate limit
\[
\mathbb{P}(c_n^{-1}e_n^*\le r)\longrightarrow 1\quad (r>0),
\]
i.e. $c_n^{-1}e_n^*\to 0$ in probability.

choices.label: C
choices.text:
In each regime (a)–(c), for every fixed $r>0$ (with $r_n=c_n r$ and $\theta$ as defined),
\[
F(n,r)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{d}\mathrm{Poisson}\bigl(r^{-\theta}\bigr).
\]
Consequently, $\mathbb{P}(e_n^*\le r_n)\to \exp(-r^{-\theta})$ for each fixed $r>0$.

choices.label: D
choices.text:
In each regime (a)–(c), for every fixed $r>0$ (with $r_n=c_n r$ and $\theta$ as defined),
\[
F(n,r)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{\mathbb{P}} r^{-\theta},
\]
and
\[
\mathbb{P}(c_n^{-1}e_n^*\le r)\longrightarrow \exp(-r^{-\theta})\quad (r>0).
\]

choices.label: E
choices.text:
In each regime (a)–(c), for every fixed $r>0$ (with $r_n=c_n r$ and $\theta$ as defined),
\[
F(n,r)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{d}\mathrm{Poisson}\bigl(r^{-1/\theta}\bigr),
\]
and
\[
\mathbb{P}(c_n^{-1}e_n^*\le r)\longrightarrow \exp\bigl(-r^{-1/\theta}\bigr)\quad (r>0),
\]
i.e. $c_n^{-1}e_n^*$ converges to a Fr\'echet law with parameter $1/\theta$.

sketch_usage_meta.label: C

ALS.justification: The stem sets up the model, regimes, and scaling, but it does not state (or strongly hint at) the Poisson/Fréchet limits or the exponent r^{-\theta}. The correct limit form only appears in the options.

TAS.justification: The question largely asks for the theorem-like limiting conclusion for a fully specified setting, so it is close to a result recall. However, it is not a pure restatement because it asks for the *strongest* conclusion, creating a hierarchy among choices (A vs weaker true C, and several near-miss falsities).

GPS.justification: Selecting A requires some reasoning about how a Poisson exceedance limit for F(n,r) implies an extreme-value (Fréchet) limit for the maximum edge length after scaling, and distinguishing distributional convergence from only pointwise CDF statements (C) or convergence in probability (D). Still, for a prepared student this is primarily recognition of a known limit theorem.

DQS.justification: Distractors reflect common failure modes: (B) incorrect degenerate maximum despite Poisson exceedances; (D) confusing Poisson convergence in distribution with convergence in probability to the mean; (E) wrong tail/exponent parameterization; (C) a deliberately weaker true statement that tests ‘strongest conclusion’ logic. They are distinct and plausible.

theorem.label: thm a

post_theorem_intro_text:
This provides a concrete
description of the distribution of shapes in this non-generic family of octic number fields and illustrates how arithmetic constraints influence the resulting
geometry of integer lattices.

\subsection{Organization}
Including the introduction, the article consists of four sections. In \S2, we recall the notion of the shape of a lattice of rank $n$ and its realization as a point in the space of shapes $\mathcal{S}_n$. We review equivalent descriptions using change-of-basis matrices and Gram matrices, and explain how the natural invariant measure on the space of shapes arises from Haar measure on $\GL_m(\mathbb{R})$. We then specialize this framework to number fields, defining the shape of a number field via the Minkowski embedding and the projection of the ring of integers onto the trace-zero subspace. Finally, we review the explicit description of integral bases for the octic Kummer extensions $L=\mathbb{Q}(i,\sqrt[4]{m})$, following the classification of \cite{quartickummer}. These bases, which depend on congruence conditions on $m$, provide the arithmetic input needed for shape computations. In \S3, we compute the Gram matrices associated to the
Minkowski lattices of the rings of integers of the octic Kummer extensions
$L=\mathbb{Q}(i,\sqrt[4]{m})$. We show that the lattice shapes are governed by the parameters $(\lambda_1, \lambda_2)$ in an asymptotic sense as $|m|\rightarrow \infty$. In Section~\S4, we study the distribution of the shape
parameters $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2)$ by counting triples $(f,g,h)\in\mathbb{Z}[i]^3$
ordered by a natural height arising from the discriminant.
We first obtain an asymptotic formula without arithmetic restrictions using
geometry-of-numbers arguments. Then we impose squarefreeness and
coprimality conditions and prove Theorem \ref{thm a}.

\subsection*{Declarations}
\begin{description}
     \item[Conflict of interest] Not applicable, there is no conflict of interest to report.
    \item[Availability of data and materials] No data was generated or analyzed in obtaining the results in this article.
\end{description}

The argument proceeds by first obtaining "an asymptotic formula without arithmetic restrictions using geometry-of-numbers arguments," and then "impos[ing] squarefreeness and coprimality conditions" to conclude and thus prove Theorem~\ref{thm a}.

mcq.question: Let $N(\mathcal R;X)$ be the counting function associated to a region $\mathcal R$ (in the given setup), and let $\hat\mu$ be the associated measure for which $\int_{\mathcal R}\hat\mu$ is defined. As $X\to\infty$, what is the strongest justified conclusion about the limit of $\frac{N(\mathcal R;X)}{X}$?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: The limit exists and satisfies $$\lim_{X\to\infty}\frac{N(\mathcal R;X)}{X}=\int_{\mathcal R}\hat\mu\,.$$

choices.label: B
choices.text:
For every region $\mathcal R$ as in the setup, one has the stronger asymptotic
\[
N(\mathcal R;X)=X\int_{\mathcal R}\hat\mu+o(X)\quad\text{as }X\to\infty.
\]

choices.label: C
choices.text: If the limit $\displaystyle\lim_{X\to\infty}\frac{N(\mathcal R;X)}{X}$ exists, then it equals $\displaystyle\int_{\mathcal R}\hat\mu$.

choices.label: D
choices.text:
One has only the upper bound
\[
\limsup_{X\to\infty}\frac{N(\mathcal R;X)}{X}\le \int_{\mathcal R}\hat\mu.
\]

choices.label: E
choices.text:
The limit exists for every $\mathcal R$ as in the setup and satisfies
\[
\lim_{X\to\infty}\frac{N(\mathcal R;X)}{X}=\int_{\overline{\mathcal R}}\hat\mu,
\]
where $\overline{\mathcal R}$ denotes the closure of $\mathcal R$.

ALS.justification: The stem introduces the objects N(R;X) and the measure \hat\mu, but does not state (or strongly hint) that N(R;X)/X converges to \int_R \hat\mu. The correct equality is not telegraphed by wording like “show that” or “it follows that,” and several plausible weaker/stronger alternatives are offered.

TAS.justification: If the “given setup” already contains (or is known to imply) an equidistribution/counting theorem, then the question is close to asking the theorem’s conclusion. However, it is not a pure restatement because it explicitly asks for the *strongest justified conclusion* among competing statements (limit vs limsup vs conditional vs stronger asymptotic vs closure issue).

GPS.justification: Selecting the “strongest justified” option forces the solver to reason about logical strength (existence of limit vs conditional equality), the difference between a limit statement and a full asymptotic with error term, and boundary/regularity subtleties (R vs \overline{R}). This is more than recognition.

DQS.justification: Distractors are plausible and target common failure modes: (B) overclaiming an error term from a limit, (C) giving only a conditional statement (weaker-true trap), (D) confusing limit equality with a one-sided limsup bound, and (E) a realistic boundary/closure regularity trap. They are distinct and aligned with typical misconceptions.

qa quality eval.overall_assessment: High-quality MCQ with no answer leakage and strong reasoning demand via a “strongest justified conclusion” comparison. The only weakness is that, depending on what is contained in the unspecified “given setup,” it may feel like recalling a known theorem rather than deriving a novel conclusion.

\begin{theorem}[Critical-window breakdown at $\beta=1$ (fixed $M$)]
		\label{thm:crit_break_sqrtN}
		Fix $\beta=1$ and let $M\in\mathbb N$ be fixed.
		Let $k=k(N)$ satisfy
		\[
		\frac{k}{\sqrt N}\longrightarrow c\in(0,\infty).
		\]
		Then there exists a deterministic constant $b=b(c,M)>0$ such that
		\[

		\qquad\text{in }\mathbb P_\xi\text{-probability}.
		\]

\begin{theorem}		\label{thm:stop_macro_Msmall}
		Fix $\beta\in(0,1)$ and assume $M=M(N)\to\infty$ with $M=o(\sqrt N)$.

		\]

	And finally, we show
	\begin{theorem}[Critical-window breakdown at $\beta=1$ (fixed $M$)]
		\label{thm:crit_break_sqrtN}
		Fix $\beta=1$ and let $M\in\mathbb N$ be fixed.
		Let $k=k(N)$ satisfy
		\[
		\frac{k}{\sqrt N}\longrightarrow c\in(0,\infty).
		\]
		Then there exists a deterministic constant $b=b(c,M)>0$ such that
		\[
		\liminf_{N\to\infty} \ d_{\mathrm{TV}}\big(\mu_N^{(k)},\pi^{\otimes k}\big)\ \ge\ b
		\qquad\text{in }\mathbb P_\xi\text{-probability}.
		\]
		In particular, propagation of chaos fails in the critical window $k\asymp \sqrt N$,
		showing that the scaling in Theorem~\ref{thm:crit_poc} is optimal.

	\end{theorem}
	\subsection{Outline of the proofs}

	A central idea in our proofs is that the Hopfield Gibbs measure admits,
	via a Hubbard--Stratonovich transformation, an explicit representation
	in terms of a mixture of product measures.

	\medskip
	\noindent\textit{Step 1: Mixture-of-products representation.}
	For fixed (quenched) patterns $(\xi^\mu)_\mu$, the quadratic Hamiltonian
	$\frac{\beta N}{2}\|m_N(\sigma)\|^2$ can be linearized by introducing an
	auxiliary Gaussian field. This standard technqie for quadratic Hamiltonians yields a representation of the form
	\[
	\mu_N(d\sigma)\;=\;\int \nu_{N,\beta}(d y)\,
	\bigotimes_{i=1}^N \mu_{y,i}(d\sigma_i),
	\]
	where $y\in\mathbb R^M$ is the Hubbard--Stratonovich field, $\nu_{N,\beta}$ is an
	explicit probability measure on $\mathbb R^M$, and $\mu_{y,i}$ is a Bernoulli law
	with bias depending on $y\cdot \xi_i$.
	Consequently, the $k$-spin marginal $\mu_N^{(k)}$ is a mixture of product
	measures on $\{-1,+1\}^k$.

	\medskip
	\noindent\textit{Step 2: Propagation of chaos reduces to stability of the mixture.}
	Conditionally on $y$, the spins are independent.
	Thus propagation of chaos for $\mu_N$ is controlled by how strongly the
	random field $y$ fluctuates under $\nu_{N,\beta}$ and by how sensitively
	the single-spin biases $\mu_{y,i}$ depend on $y$.
	Quantitatively, we compare the mixture to the unbiased product law
	$\pi^{\otimes k}$ in total variation distance.

	\medskip
	\noindent\textit{Step 3: High temperature $\beta<1$.}
	In the regime $\beta<1$, the Hubbard--Stratonovich field typically remains
	of order one and concentrates near the origin.
	A Taylor expansion of the single-spin biases and a control of
	$\nu_{N,\beta}$ show that correlations between $k$ spins are of order
	$kM/N$, yielding Theorem~\ref{thm:highT} under the condition $kM/N\to0$.
	For macroscopic $k$ (with $k/N\to\rho$), the same representation allows us
	to exhibit order-one correlations induced by the random field, which leads
	to strong breakdown in total variation (Theorem~\ref{thm:stop_macro_Msmall})
	under the stated assumptions on $M$.

	\medskip
	\noindent\textit{Step 4: Critical temperature $\beta=1$ and the critical window.}
	At criticality, the mixing measure $\nu_{N,1}$ develops non-Gaussian
	fluctuations on the scale $N^{-1/4}$, reflecting the well-known
	critical behavior of the overlap.
	This amplification of the mixing fluctuations reduces the admissible growth
	of the marginals to $k=o(N^{1/4})$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:crit_poc}).
	Moreover, when $k\asymp \sqrt N$, the mixture retains a nontrivial
	amount of randomness that produces correlations bounded away from zero,
	yielding a breakdown of propagation of chaos in the critical window
	(Theorem~\ref{thm:crit_break_sqrtN}) and hence the optimality of the scaling.

mcq.question:
Let u solve the reaction–diffusion Cauchy problem

u_t = Δu + f(u),  (x,y) ∈ ℝ^{n-1}×ℝ, t>0;   u(x,y,0)=u_0(x,y).

Assume (F) and
(1) liminf_{y→−∞} inf_{x∈ℝ^{n-1}} u_0(x,y) > 0,
(2) c = c_* > 2\sqrt{f'(0)}, and limsup_{y→∞} sup_{x∈ℝ^{n-1}} u_0(x,y)e^{−λ_1 y} < ∞ for some λ_1 < λ_+.

As t→∞, what is the strongest conclusion about the asymptotic profile of u and the geometry/dynamics of the level set {u=Φ_c(0)}, including the comparison with the solution of the forced mean-curvature-type problem (MCF)? Also, which part of the conclusion remains valid if instead of (1)–(2) one assumes
liminf_{y→−∞} inf_{x∈ℝ^{n-1}} u_0(x,y) > 1−δ_0,
0 < liminf_{y→∞} inf_{x∈ℝ^{n-1}} u_0(x,y)/Φ_c(y), and limsup_{y→∞} sup_{x∈ℝ^{n-1}} u_0(x,y)/Φ_c(y) < ∞ for some c ≥ c_*?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text:
There exist T>0 and a smooth function γ=γ(x,t) such that:
(i) for all t≥T,
{(x,y,t) ∈ ℝ^{n-1}×ℝ×[T,∞) : u(x,y,t)=Φ_c(0)} = {y=γ(x,t)},
and
lim_{t→∞} sup_{(x,y)∈ℝ^n} |u(x,y,t) − Φ_c(y−γ(x,t))| = 0.
(ii) for every ε>0 there exists τ_ε∈[T,∞) such that, if U(x,t) solves
U_t/\sqrt{1+|∇_x U|^2} = div(∇_x U/\sqrt{1+|∇_x U|}) + c_*  on ℝ^{n-1}×(0,∞),
U(x,0)=γ(x,τ_ε),
then
sup_{x∈ℝ^{n-1},\, t≥τ_ε} |γ(x,t) − U(x,t−τ_ε)| ≤ ε.
Moreover, the entire assertion in (i) (the level-set graph representation and the uniform convergence to Φ_c(y−γ(x,t))) still holds under the alternative assumptions with liminf_{y→−∞}inf_x u_0(x,y)>1−δ_0 and two-sided bounds on u_0(x,y)/Φ_c(y) as y→∞ for some c≥c_*.

theorem.label: thm:deux-bulles

sketch:
The authors give an ``\subsection{Outline of the proof}'' for Theorem~\ref{thm:deux-bulles}. They study solutions close to a sum of two bubbles via the modulation decomposition
\[
 u(t)=e^{i\zeta(t)}W_{\mu(t)}+e^{i\theta(t)}W_{\lambda(t)}+g(t),
\]
with ``$\zeta(t)$ close to $-\frac{\pi}{2}$, $\mu(t)\simeq 1$, $\theta(t)\sim 0$, $\lambda(t)\ll 1$ and $\|g(t)\|_{\mathcal E}\ll 1$.'' The main tools are stated to be ``modulation analysis, bootstrap argument and topological argument.''

Key steps (as described):
\begin{itemize}
\item (Section~\ref{sec:variational}) Recall lemmas; state ``the spectral properties of the linearized operator $Z_{\theta,\lambda}$'' and ``coercivity of the energy near a two-bubble,'' which are ``very important to estimate $g$''; they ``use the energy conservation to deal with this.''
\item (Section~\ref{sec:mod}) Estimate modulation parameters by imposing orthogonality conditions so that ``the terms linear in $g$ in the modulation equations disappeared'' (with ``essentially a unique choice"). Under bootstrap assumptions, Lemma~\ref{lem:mod} gives bounds on the evolution of modulation parameters, aiming to ``improve these bounds, thus closing the bootstrap.'' To improve the bound on $\|g\|_{\mathcal E}$ they use Lemma~\ref{lem:proper} to ``control the unstable components.''
\item (Section~\ref{sec:boot}) Prove Theorem~\ref{thm:deux-bulles}: first use the implicit function theorem to obtain the modulation decomposition; then, ``combining with virial correction'' (to improve the bound \eqref{eq:bootstrap-theta} on $\theta(t)$) they close the bootstrap for modulation parameters. They explain that the virial correction ``allows us to gain a small constant on the right hand side of \eqref{eq:mod-th}, which is decisive for closing the bootstrap.'' Linear instabilities are handled by ``a classical topological argument based on the Brouwer fixed point theorem.'' ``Finally, we prove Theorem~\ref{thm:deux-bulles}."
\end{itemize}

mcq.question:
Consider the Hartree equation on \(\mathbb R^N\)
\[
 i\partial_t u+\Delta u+\bigl(|x|^{-4}*|u|^2\bigr)u=0,\qquad f(u):=\bigl(|x|^{-4}*|u|^2\bigr)u,
\]
with values in an energy space \(\mathcal E\). Let \(W\) be a given profile and \(W_\lambda\) its scaling, and define
\[
\kappa:=\Bigl(\frac{2C_1}{3(N-6)C_2}\Bigr)^{\frac{2}{N-6}}.
\]
As \(t\to-\infty\), what is the strongest asymptotic conclusion (including existence) that can be asserted for a solution \(u(t)\)?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text:
There exist \(T_0\in\mathbb R\) and a solution \(u:(-\infty,T_0]\to\mathcal E\) of \(i\partial_t u+\Delta u+(|x|^{-4}*|u|^2)u=0\) such that
\[
\lim_{t\to-\infty}\Big\|u(t)-\bigl(-iW+W_{\kappa|t|^{-\frac{2}{N-6}}}\bigr)\Big\|_{\mathcal E}=0,
\]
with \(\kappa=\bigl(\tfrac{2C_1}{3(N-6)C_2}\bigr)^{\tfrac{2}{N-6}}\).

choices.label: B
choices.text:
There exist \(T_0\in\mathbb R\) and a solution \(u:(-\infty,T_0]\to\mathcal E\) of \(i\partial_t u+\Delta u+(|x|^{-4}*|u|^2)u=0\) such that
\[
\lim_{t\to-\infty}\Big\|u(t)-\bigl(-iW+W_{\kappa |t|^{-\frac{2}{N-6}}}\bigr)\Big\|_{\mathcal E}=0,
\]
where \(\kappa=\bigl(\tfrac{2C_1}{3(N-6)C_2}\bigr)^{\tfrac{2}{N-6}}\), and moreover the convergence holds with the quantitative rate
\[
\Big\|u(t)-\bigl(-iW+W_{\kappa |t|^{-\frac{2}{N-6}}}\bigr)\Big\|_{\mathcal E}\lesssim |t|^{-\frac{N-1}{2(N-6)}}\quad\text{as }t\to-\infty.
\]

choices.label: C
choices.text:
There exist \(T_0\in\mathbb R\) and a solution \(u:(-\infty,T_0]\to\mathcal E\) of \(i\partial_t u+\Delta u+(|x|^{-4}*|u|^2)u=0\) such that
\[
\lim_{t\to-\infty}\|u(t)+iW\|_{\mathcal E}=0.
\]

choices.label: D
choices.text:
There exist \(T_0\in\mathbb R\) and a solution \(u:(-\infty,T_0]\to\mathcal E\) of \(i\partial_t u+\Delta u+(|x|^{-4}*|u|^2)u=0\) such that
\[
\lim_{t\to-\infty}\Big\|u(t)-\bigl(e^{i\zeta_\infty}W+W_{\kappa |t|^{-\frac{2}{N-6}}}\bigr)\Big\|_{\mathcal E}=0
\]
for some constant phase \(\zeta_\infty\in\mathbb R\), with \(\kappa=\bigl(\tfrac{2C_1}{3(N-6)C_2}\bigr)^{\tfrac{2}{N-6}}\).

choices.label: E
choices.text:
There exist \(T_0\in\mathbb R\) and a solution \(u:(-\infty,T_0]\to\mathcal E\) of \(i\partial_t u+\Delta u+(|x|^{-4}*|u|^2)u=0\) such that
\[
\lim_{t\to-\infty}\Big\|u(t)-\bigl(-iW+W_{\kappa |t|^{-\frac{2}{N-6}}}\bigr)\Big\|_{\mathcal E}=0,
\]
but with \(\kappa\) replaced by an arbitrary constant \(\kappa'>0\) (i.e. for every \(\kappa'>0\) such a solution exists).

theorem.content:
\label{thm:counterexample}
Fix any constant $c$ with $0<c<\frac{1}{2\log 2}$. Let $p$ be prime and let $A\subseteq \mathbb{F}_p$ be a uniformly random $k$-element subset with $k=\lfloor \log_2 p + c\log\log p\rfloor$. Then
\[
\mathbb{P}\bigl(\Sigma(A)=\mathbb{F}_p\bigr)\longrightarrow 0 \qquad (p\to\infty).
\]
theorem.label: thm:counterexample

ref_dict.prob:EP543:
\begin{problem}\label{prob:EP543}
Define $f(N)$ to be the minimal $k$ such that the following holds: if $G$ is an abelian group of size $N$ and
$A\subseteq G$ is a uniformly random $k$-element subset, then with probability at least $1/2$ every element of $G$
can be written in the form $\sum_{x\in S}x$ for some $S\subseteq A$. Is
\[
f(N) \le \log_2 N + o(\log\log N)\,?
\]
\end{problem}
ref_dict.prop:poisson-miss:
\begin{proposition}\label{prop:poisson-miss}
Fix $m\in\{1,2\}$. For any $B\subseteq\F_p^\times$ with $|B|=m$,
\[
\PP\bigl(X_B=0\bigr)=e^{-m\lambda}\,(1+o(1))\qquad (p\to\infty),
\]
where the $o(1)$ is uniform over all such $B$.
\end{proposition}

post_theorem_intro_text:
This provides a quantitative bound for primes, which answers Problem~\ref{prob:EP543} in the negative.

\begin{corollary}
For all sufficiently large primes $p$, it holds that
\[
f(p)\ge \log_2 p + \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\originalleft(\frac{1}{2\log 2}+o(1)\aftergroup\egroup\originalright)\log\log p.
\]
\end{corollary}

\smallskip

\subsection{Declaration of AI usage}

The interest of this work lies not only in the mathematical results presented but also in the process by which it was obtained, with large language models serving as a major research assistant.
For transparency and reproducibility, we provide the AI-assisted workflow below.\footnote{For a public record of the development, see the second author's comments posted at 13:12 on 21 Jan 2026 and 11:37 on 23 Jan 2026 in the forum thread at \url{https://www.erdosproblems.com/forum/thread/543}.}

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
\item In an initial chat, we asked ChatGPT-5.2 Pro to search for a counterexample to the Erd\H{o}s problem stated in~\cite{EP543} (i.e., the inequality in Problem~\ref{prob:EP543}).
The model returned a proposed counterexample together with an accompanying argument.

\item In a separate chat, we asked ChatGPT-5.2 Pro to verify the proof from the first session.
It reported a serious gap that invalidated the argument as written.

\item We then asked the second chat session to repair the argument.
It produced a patched version that indeed disproves the inequality in Problem~\ref{prob:EP543}.
The AI-generated proof, with minimal edits for readability, is available at~\cite{Git}.

\item Motivated by the upper bound due to Erd\H{o}s and R\'{e}nyi~\cite{ErRe65}, we observed that for prime $p$ one can obtain a quantitative lower bound, rather than only the qualitative disproof produced by the AI. 
By strengthening several steps of the AI-generated argument, we derived the quantitative lower bound for $f(p)$ stated in Theorem~\ref{thm:counterexample}.
\end{enumerate}

We emphasize that step~(iv), as well as the writing of the paper, was carried out by the human authors.
Related papers on AI-assisted solutions to Erd\H{o}s problems have appeared recently; see, for example,
Sothanaphan~\cite{Sothanaphan26c}, Barreto et al.~\cite{BarretoKangKimKovacZhang26}, and Feng et al.~\cite{FengTrinhEtAl26}.
In our view, this work serves as an illustrative case study of AI-assisted use of the probabilistic method and linear algebra in combinatorics.

\subsection{Paper organization}
The rest of the paper is organized as follows. Section~\ref{sec:preliminaries} collects notation and several auxiliary lemmas. In Section~\ref{sec:proof} we prove Theorem~\ref{thm:counterexample} by first establishing the key Poisson-like estimate, Proposition~\ref{prop:poisson-miss}, and then combining it with a second-moment argument. Section~\ref{sec:concluding} contains several concluding remarks.

mcq.question:
Fix $s>0$, $T>0$, and dimension $d\in\{2,3\}$. Consider the incompressible MHD system on $\mathbb{R}^d$
\[
\begin{cases}
\partial_t u+u\cdot\nabla u+\nabla p=b\cdot\nabla b,\\
\partial_t b-\Delta b+u\cdot\nabla b=b\cdot\nabla u,\\
\operatorname{div}u=\operatorname{div}b=0,\\
(u,b)|_{t=0}=(u_0,b_0).
\end{cases}
\]
The data-to-solution map sends initial data from a bounded subset of $H^s(\mathbb{R}^d)\times H^s(\mathbb{R}^d)$ into $C([0,T],H^s(\mathbb{R}^d))\times C([0,T],H^s(\mathbb{R}^d))$. For arbitrary $\gamma>0$ and any constant magnetic field ${\bf B}_0\in\mathbb{R}^d$, which limiting/asymptotic statement as $\lambda\to\infty$ (including the strongest conclusion about uniform continuity) is justified?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text:
The data-to-solution map is non-uniformly continuous (from a bounded subset of $H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^d)\times H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ into $C([0,T],H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^d))\times C([0,T],H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^d))$). More precisely, for any $\gamma>0$ and any constant ${\bf B}_0\in\mathbb{R}^d$, there exist two families of solutions $\{(u^{+1,\lambda},b^{+1,\lambda})\}_{\lambda}$ and $\{(u^{-1,\lambda},b^{-1,\lambda})\}_{\lambda}$ such that
1) $(u^{\pm1,\lambda},\, b^{\pm1,\lambda}-{\bf B}_0)\in C([0,T],H^s(\mathbb{R}^d))\times C([0,T],H^s(\mathbb{R}^d))$;
2) $\|u^{\pm1,\lambda}(0)\|_{H^s}+\|b^{\pm1,\lambda}(0)-{\bf B}_0\|_{H^s}\le \gamma$;
3) at $t=0$, $\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\|u^{+1,\lambda}(0)-u^{-1,\lambda}(0)\|_{H^s}=0$, while for each fixed $t>0$,
\[
\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\|u^{+1,\lambda}(t)-u^{-1,\lambda}(t)\|_{H^s}\ge c\,\gamma\,|\sin t|,
\]
where $c=c(s,d)>0$ depends only on $s$ and $d$.

choices.label: B
choices.text:
The data-to-solution map is non-uniformly continuous. More precisely, for any $\gamma>0$ and any constant ${\bf B}_0\in\mathbb{R}^d$, there exist two families of solutions $\{(u^{+1,\lambda},b^{+1,\lambda})\}_{\lambda}$ and $\{(u^{-1,\lambda},b^{-1,\lambda})\}_{\lambda}$ such that
1) $(u^{\pm1,\lambda},\, b^{\pm1,\lambda}-{\bf B}_0)\in C([0,T],H^s(\mathbb{R}^d))\times C([0,T],H^s(\mathbb{R}^d))$;
2) $\|u^{\pm1,\lambda}(0)\|_{H^s}+\|b^{\pm1,\lambda}(0)-{\bf B}_0\|_{H^s}\le \gamma$;
3) at $t=0$, $\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\|u^{+1,\lambda}(0)-u^{-1,\lambda}(0)\|_{H^s}=0$, and moreover for evolution times $t>0$ one has the stronger limit
\[
\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\|u^{+1,\lambda}(t)-u^{-1,\lambda}(t)\|_{H^s}=c\,\gamma\,|\sin t|,
\]
where $c=c(s,d)>0$ depends only on $s$ and $d$.

choices.label: C
D
choices.text:
The data-to-solution map is uniformly continuous from bounded subsets of $H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^d)\times H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ into $C([0,T],H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^d))\times C([0,T],H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^d))$. Equivalently, for every $\gamma>0$ and every constant ${\bf B}_0\in\mathbb{R}^d$ there is a modulus $\omega$ (depending only on $s,d,T,\gamma$) such that for any two solutions with $\|u(0)\|_{H^s}+\|b(0)-{\bf B}_0\|_{H^s}\le\gamma$ and $\|\tilde u(0)\|_{H^s}+\|\tilde b(0)-{\bf B}_0\|_{H^s}\le\gamma$ one has
\[
\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\big(\|u(t)-\tilde u(t)\|_{H^s}+\|b(t)-\tilde b(t)\|_{H^s}\big)\le \omega\big(\|u(0)-\tilde u(0)\|_{H^s}+\|b(0)-\tilde b(0)\|_{H^s}\big).
\]
In particular, no pair of sequences with $\|u^{\pm1,\lambda}(0)\|_{H^s}+\|b^{\pm1,\lambda}(0)-{\bf B}_0\|_{H^s}\le\gamma$ can satisfy $\|u^{+1,\lambda}(0)-u^{-1,\lambda}(0)\|_{H^s}\to0$ while $\liminf_{\lambda\to\infty}\|u^{+1,\lambda}(t)-u^{-1,\lambda}(t)\|_{H^s}\ge c\gamma|\sin t|$ for any fixed $t>0$.

choices.label: E
choices.text:
The data-to-solution map is non-uniformly continuous. More precisely, for any $\gamma>0$ and any constant ${\bf B}_0\in\mathbb{R}^d$, there exist two families of solutions $\{(u^{+1,\lambda},b^{+1,\lambda})\}_{\lambda}$ and $\{(u^{-1,\lambda},b^{-1,\lambda})\}_{\lambda}$ such that
1) $(u^{\pm1,\lambda},\, b^{\pm1,\lambda}-{\bf B}_0)\in C([0,T],H^s(\mathbb{R}^d))\times C([0,T],H^s(\mathbb{R}^d))$;
2) $\|u^{\pm1,\lambda}(0)\|_{H^s}+\|b^{\pm1,\lambda}(0)-{\bf B}_0\|_{H^s}\le \gamma$;
3) at $t=0$, $\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\big(\|u^{+1,\lambda}(0)-u^{-1,\lambda}(0)\|_{H^s}+\|b^{+1,\lambda}(0)-b^{-1,\lambda}(0)\|_{H^s}\big)=0$, while for each fixed $t>0$,
\[
\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\big(\|u^{+1,\lambda}(t)-u^{-1,\lambda}(t)\|_{H^s}+\|b^{+1,\lambda}(t)-b^{-1,\lambda}(t)\|_{H^s}\big)\ge c\,\gamma\,|\sin t|,
\]
where $c=c(s,d)>0$ depends only on $s$ and $d$.

Our proof approach is based on similar results 
for the contiguous model $\mathbb{H}(n,q), q=p^s$ which are already known in the literature. Specifically, the existence of $m(F,c)$ such that 
\begin{align*}
\frac{{\rm MinM}(\mathbb{H}(n,q),F)}{n}
\to m(F,c),
\end{align*}
is already known~\cite{shabanov2021maximum} based on the combinatorial interpolation technique introduced in~\cite{bayati2010combinatorial} and used
for establishing the existence of
such limits.
For similar contiguity reasons 
we also have that  
$m(F,c)=0$ when $c$ is 
sufficiently small positive 
constant $c$, and $m(F,c)>0$ when $c$ is sufficiently large. 
The former claim  is
obtained by choosing $c$ small enough so that
the  random graph $\mathbb{H}(n,q)$ does not contain
a giant component. In this case the 
locally tree-like
structure of the graph allows for cutting nearly
every $F$-edge  of the graph. Conversely, when
$c$ is sufficiently large, the 
non-existence of near
perfect bipartition follows from a simple union
bound. We regard these observations as folklore 
and will not provide a formal verification of 
these claims.

We conjecture that the value 
${\rm MinM}(\mathbb{G}(n,p),F){n}$ also undergoes a different type of phase transition. Specifically, we conjecture the existence of $c^*$ which 
depends on $F$ only such that this value is $0$ w.h.p. as $n\to\infty$
when $c<c^*$, and is positive  when $c>c^*$ also w.h.p.
The basis for this conjecture is a similar conjecture for random K-SAT (and several other related models such as proper coloring
of a random graph), which was proven for large $K$~\cite{ding2022proof}, but is still open for general $K$.

Our next result concerns obtaining explicit 
asymptotic limit
values when the size of the host graph $F$ grows.  
Introduce a short-hand notation
\begin{align*}
\kappa(F,c,s,r)={c^s\over 2^{r-1}{\rm aut}(F)}.
\end{align*}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm-limit}
   Under the assumption of \Cref{thm-convergence},
\begin{align*}
       m(F,c)=\kappa(F,c,s,r)+
    (1+o_r(1))\sqrt{(2\log 2)\kappa(F,c,s,r)}
       +o_{c}(c^{s/2}).
   \end{align*}
\end{theorem} 
Namely, we obtain explicit limit values when both the number of nodes of the host graph $F$ and the leading coefficient $c$ of the random graph 
parameter diverge to infinity. The proof inspiration
is based on large-$p$
approximation technique
for $p$-spin glass models employed recently
in~\cite{gamarnik2025shattering}, and porting these
results to sparse random graphs as was done 
in~\cite{dms2017} 
and~\cite{sen2018optimization}. The latter two works relate $p$-spin models to sparse graphs using the Lindeberg's interpolation method.
Instead, we develop relevant asymptotics directly for sparse graphs using the second 
moment method employed 
in~\cite{gamarnik2025shattering}
for the mean field $p$-spin model.

\paragraph{Organization} The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In \Cref{sec-hypergraph-coupling}, we introduce a coupling between the random $F$-graph and the Erdős–Rényi random graph, and prove \Cref{thm-convergence}. In \Cref{sec-spinglass}, we reduce the study of \( m(F,p) \) to the analysis of the maximum of a family of Gaussian random variables. Section~\ref{sec-maximizer}  provides auxiliary results that en route to deriving this maximum. Finally, we prove \Cref{thm-limit} in \Cref{sec-proof}.

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: There exists a constant $m(F,c)$ (depending only on $F$ and $c$) such that, with high probability as $n\to\infty$, \[\frac{{\rm MinM}(\mathbb{G}(n,p),F)}{n}\to m(F,c).\]

choices.label: B

There exists a constant $m(F,c)>0$ (depending only on $F$ and $c$) such that 
\[
\mathbb{E}\Big[\frac{{\rm MinM}(\mathbb{G}(n,p),F)}{n}\Big]\to m(F,c)
\]
as $n\to\infty$.

choices.label: C
choices.text:
There exists a deterministic function $m(F,c,n)$ (depending only on $F,c,n$) such that, with high probability as $n\to\infty$, 
\[
\frac{{\rm MinM}(\mathbb{G}(n,p),F)}{n}-m(F,c,n)\to 0.
\]

choices.label: D
choices.text:
There exists a constant $m(F,c)$ (depending only on $F$ and $c$) such that, with high probability as $n\to\infty$, 
\[
\frac{{\rm MinM}(\mathbb{G}(n,p),F)}{n}\to m(F,c)
\]
holds for every choice of $p=cn^{-\alpha}$ with $\alpha=1/\rd_1(F)$ and every associated $q=p^s$.

choices.label: E
choices.text:
There exists a constant $m(F,c)$ (depending only on $F$ and $c$) such that, with high probability as $n\to\infty$, 
\[
\frac{{\rm MinM}(\mathbb{H}(n,q),F)}{n}\to m(F,c)
\quad\text{and hence}\quad
\frac{{\rm MinM}(\mathbb{G}(n,p),F)}{n}\to m(F,c)
\]
for $p=cn^{-1/\rd_1(F)}$ and $q=p^s=c^sn^{1-r}$.

post_theorem_intro_text:
\subsection{Main ideas and comparison with related work}
Our analysis uses a spatial-dynamics and Hamiltonian formulation of the traveling-wave Euler system,
followed by a nonlinear transformation that rectifies the free-boundary conditions and the symplectic
structure. This leads to an infinite-dimensional reversible Hamiltonian system which, along a
distinguished curve in parameter space, has a two-dimensional center subspace. We verify the resolvent
bounds needed for Mielke's center-manifold theorem, obtain a finite-dimensional reduced canonical system,
and identify a KdV-type normal form admitting a homoclinic orbit after a long-wave scaling and a cubic expansion of the reduced Hamiltonian. The persistence of this orbit yields solitary waves for the
original free-boundary Euler equations.

Our approach is complementary to Rowan--Wan \cite{rowan2024two}, who constructed pure-capillary solitary waves in infinite depth via a Babenko-type boundary-integral equation; the infinite-depth geometry leads to a different nonlocal operator and dispersive structure. We also note that Kharif--Abid--Chen--Hsu \cite{kharif2025nonlinear} derived amplitude equations predicting finite-depth capillary solitary waves with vorticity by formal asymptotics and matching arguments.

\subsection{Organization of the paper}
The rest of the paper is organized as follows. In Section~\ref{sec:formulation} we introduce the traveling-wave
reduction and the Hamiltonian/spatial-dynamics formulation. In Section~\ref{sec:center} we carry out the center-manifold
reduction and derive the reduced canonical system. In Section~\ref{sec:normalform} we compute the normal form and prove
the existence of a homoclinic orbit, and we lift the construction to a solitary wave of the full Euler system.

mcq.question:
Let $c\neq 0$ and assume the parameters satisfy $\dfrac{\omega d}{c}=1+\varepsilon$ for a sufficiently small absolute constant $\varepsilon>0$ and $\dfrac{\sigma}{c^{2}d}>\tfrac13$. Consider the free-boundary system
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\phi_{xx}+\phi_{yy}=0 && \text{in } -d<y<\eta(t,x),\\
&\phi_y=0 && \text{on } y=-d,\\
&\eta_t=\phi_y-(\phi_x-\omega \eta)\eta_x && \text{on } y=\eta(t,x),\\
&\phi_t+\frac12(\phi_x^2+\phi_y^2)-\omega\eta\,\phi_x+\omega\psi
-\frac{\sigma\,\eta_{xx}}{(1+\eta_x^2)^{3/2}}=0 && \text{on } y=\eta(t,x).
\end{aligned}
\]
As $\varepsilon\to 0^+$, what is the strongest justified conclusion about the existence of a solitary wave of speed $c$ and the asymptotic expansion of its profile $\eta(\xi)$?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text:
Under these assumptions, the system admits a $C^2$ solitary wave solution with velocity $c$. Moreover, its solitary-wave profile has the asymptotic expansion
\[
\eta(\xi)=d\,\varepsilon\, Q\!\left(\varepsilon^{\frac12}\left(\frac{\sigma}{c^2d}-\frac13\right)^{-\frac12}\frac{\xi}{d}\right)+O(\varepsilon^2)\qquad (\varepsilon\to 0^+),
\]
where $Q(\bar x)=-3\,\mathrm{sech}^2(\bar x/2)$ and $Q$ solves the steady KdV equation $Q''=Q+\tfrac12 Q^2$.

choices.label: B
choices.text:
Under these assumptions, the system admits a $C^2$ solitary wave solution with velocity $c$. Moreover, its solitary-wave profile has the asymptotic expansion
\[
\eta(\xi)=d\,\varepsilon\, Q\!\left(\varepsilon^{\frac12}\left(\frac{\sigma}{c^2d}-\frac13\right)^{-\frac12}\frac{\xi}{d}\right)+O(\varepsilon^3)\qquad (\varepsilon\to 0^+),
\]
where $Q(\bar x)=-3\,\mathrm{sech}^2(\bar x/2)$ and $Q$ solves the steady KdV equation $Q''=Q+\tfrac12 Q^2$.

choices.label: C
choices.text:
Under these assumptions, the system admits a $C^2$ solitary wave solution with velocity $c$. Furthermore, as $\varepsilon\to 0^+$ the leading-order solitary-wave profile is governed by the steady KdV homoclinic, in the sense that
\[
\eta(\xi)=d\,\varepsilon\, Q\!\left(\varepsilon^{\frac12}\left(\frac{\sigma}{c^2d}-\frac13\right)^{-\frac12}\frac{\xi}{d}\right)+o(\varepsilon)\qquad (\varepsilon\to 0^+),
\]
where $Q(\bar x)=-3\,\mathrm{sech}^2(\bar x/2)$ solves $Q''=Q+\tfrac12 Q^2$.

choices.label: D
choices.text:
Under these assumptions, for each sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$ the system admits a $C^2$ solitary wave solution with velocity $c$, and the remainder in the KdV asymptotic expansion can be chosen uniformly as $\frac{\sigma}{c^2d}\downarrow \frac13$, namely
\[
\eta(\xi)=d\,\varepsilon\, Q\!\left(\varepsilon^{\frac12}\left(\frac{\sigma}{c^2d}-\frac13\right)^{-\frac12}\frac{\xi}{d}\right)+O(\varepsilon^2)
\]
with an $O(\varepsilon^2)$ constant independent of $\left(\frac{\sigma}{c^2d}-\frac13\right)$.

choices.label: E
choices.text:
Under these assumptions, the system admits a $C^2$ solitary wave solution with velocity $c$. Moreover, its solitary-wave profile has the asymptotic expansion
\[
\eta(\xi)=d\,\varepsilon\, Q\!\left(\varepsilon\left(\frac{\sigma}{c^2d}-\frac13\right)^{-\frac12}\frac{\xi}{d}\right)+O(\varepsilon^2)\qquad (\varepsilon\to 0^+),
\]
where $Q(\bar x)=-3\,\mathrm{sech}^2(\bar x/2)$ and $Q$ solves the steady KdV equation $Q''=Q+\tfrac12 Q^2$.

\begin{remark}\label{rem:Baakeresult}
    In \cite{BaakeGaehlerGohlke2025}, the authors introduce the notion of a \emph{discrepancy inflation} for a self-similar, nonperiodic topological tiling dynamical system $(\mathbb{X},\mathbb{R}^d)$ with pure-point spectrum generated by a primitive inflation, using it to establish lower and upper bounds for the amorphic complexity of $(\mathbb{X},\mathbb{R}^d)$. Though their work focuses on tilings (rather than the symbolic setting), it is easy to see that, for a substitution $\varphi$ of constant length, their discrepancy inflation corresponds to our discrepancy substitution.

    By translating their main result (\cite[Thm.\ 4.13 \& Prop.\ 4.14]{BaakeGaehlerGohlke2025}) to our framework, we obtain the following bounds:
    \[
        \frac{\log k}{\log k - \log \lambda_{min}} \leq \oac(X_{\varphi}) \leq \frac{\log k}{\log k - \log \lambda_s},
    \]
    where $\lambda_s$ (resp.\ $\lambda_{min}$) denotes the maximal (resp.\ minimal) growth rate of letters in the discrepancy substitution $\varphi_s$, and $k$ is the length of the substitution. If $\lambda_s = \lambda_{min}$, this yields a closed-form expression for the amorphic complexity of $X_{\varphi}$. However, in general, one typically expects that $\lambda_{min} < \lambda_s$; see e.g.\ Example~\ref{ex:sep_substitution_not_irreducible}.
\end{remark}

post_theorem_intro_text:
In particular, Theorem~\ref{introthm:tameness} yields that a system $X_{\varphi}$ is null iff it is tame (recall that nullness always implies tameness); to the best of our knowledge, this is a new result even in case of a binary alphabet. Furthermore, at the end of the introduction of \cite{FuhrmannKellendonkYassawi2024}, it is pointed out that \cite[Thm.~1.2]{FuhrmannKellendonkYassawi2024} together with \cite[Thm.~1.1]{FuhrmannGroeger2020} yields the equivalence of (i) and (iii) in the binary case. This means that, concerning this equivalence, Theorem~\ref{introthm:tameness} extends this observation to the full general case in the minimal setting.

Theorem~\ref{introthm:tameness} offers a natural interpretation of tameness and nullness in the context of minimal automatic systems. As shown in \cite[Cor.~1.3]{FuhrmannGroeger2020}, amorphic complexity of such systems is either $0$ or lies in the interval $[1, \infty]$. Furthermore, it is straightforward to demonstrate that amorphic complexity can attain a dense set of values in $[1, \infty)$ in the class of minimal automatic systems over a fixed alphabet of size at least two (see Proposition~\ref{prop:denseness}). Beyond the trivial case where amorphic complexity is $0$ (corresponding to periodic behaviour), this reveals a complexity gap between $0$ and $1$, with tame and null systems occupying exactly the minimal nontrivial complexity level of $1$.

To establish Theorem \ref{introthm:tameness} we need to determine amorphic complexity for arbitrary minimal automatic systems.
For this, to each primitive substitution $\varphi$ of constant length we associate its \emph{discrepancy substitution} $\varphi_s$ and define the \emph{discrepancy rate} $\lambda_s$ of $\varphi$ as the dominant eigenvalue of the incidence matrix of $\varphi_s$ (see Section \ref{sec:discrepancysubstitution}). 
The discrepancy substitution $\varphi_s$ is straightforward to compute; however, in general, it is not primitive, which makes its analysis considerably more delicate.
For this reason, we introduce suitable dynamically defined pseudometrics that allow for a refined analysis of the discrepancy structure.
With this we derive a closed formula for the amorphic complexity of any minimal automatic systems, showing, in particular, that it always exists.

\begin{introtheorem}\label{introthm:ac_of_automatic_systems} Let $\varphi$ be a primitive substitution of length $k\geqslant 2$.  The amorphic complexity of $X_{\varphi}$ is given by
\[\ac(X_{\varphi})=\frac{\log k}{\log k - \log \lambda_s},\]
where $\lambda_s$ is the discrepancy rate of $\varphi$.\footnote{Assuming the usual conventions when dividing by 0 or $\infty$ and $-\log 0 = \infty$.}
\end{introtheorem}

We note that in case of a binary alphabet, Theorem~\ref{introthm:ac_of_automatic_systems} coincides with \cite[Thm.~1.1]{FuhrmannGroeger2020}. Moreover, for general alphabets, \cite{FuhrmannGroeger2020} also provides a potential algorithm to compute concrete lower and upper bounds for the lower and upper amorphic complexity of $X_\varphi$, whereas \cite{BaakeGaehlerGohlke2025} gives improved lower and upper bounds; see also Remark~\ref{rem:Baakeresult}.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section~\ref{sec:setup} we collect the necessary preliminaries. In Section~\ref{sec:discrepancytools} we introduce the discrepancy substitution and new dynamically generated pseudometrics, which serve as the main technical tools throughout the paper. In Section~\ref{sec:complexityofsubstitution} we prove Theorem~\ref{introthm:ac_of_automatic_systems} concerning the formula for the amorphic complexity. Finally, in Section~\ref{sec:tamenessandnullness} we establish Theorem~\ref{introthm:tameness}.

theorem.label: thm:intro-main

post_theorem_intro_text:
Although the global Stokes groupoid \eqref{eq:intro-global-stokes} is defined intrinsically as a $2$-fiber product,
the main point of this paper is to provide an explicit small strict presenter for it, adapted to SNC depth and Kummer descent.
Concretely, we:
\begin{itemize}
\item construct a strict \v{C}ech--Stokes collar groupoid $\G_C$ and identify the correct collar moduli as $\operatorname{Sec}(\pi)$
(rather than $\Rep_r(\G_C)$), making the Stokes layer strictly functorial and cover-based;
\item build the explicit $2$-pushout presenter $\G_{\Phi,n}$ and prove that it computes global Stokes objects via the torsorial gluing problem
in \Cref{thm:intro-main};
\item make the tame/Kummer layer along depth strata functorial at the level of presenters, enabling explicit descent constraints
and, in particular, a hands-on description in terms of equivariant cocycles;
\item provide finite skeletal models (invariant up to Morita equivalence, with contractible ambiguity) and an explicit
generators-and-relations/chamber-complex description in SNC corners, solving the local presentation problem highlighted in
Problem~12.3.
\end{itemize}

Theorem~\Cref{thm:intro-main} makes it possible to treat global Stokes objects using a concrete presenter:
questions about existence, comparison, and descent can be translated into torsors and nonabelian \v{C}ech cocycles
on an explicit skeleton underlying $\G_{\Phi,n}$.
We record three consequences that will be used later; each is proved in the indicated section.

\begin{corollary} \label{cor:intro-morita}
If one replaces the interior and collar covers by refinements, the resulting pushout groupoid $G'_{\Phi,n}$
is Morita equivalent to $\G_{\Phi,n}$; in particular the associated torsorial representation groupoids are equivalent:
$\Rep_r(G'_{\Phi,n})\simeq \Rep_r(\G_{\Phi,n})$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary} \label{cor:intro-kummer}
Along a depth-$k$ stratum of $D$, the Kummer cover $X^{\log}_n\to X^{\log}$ has deck group $(\mu_n)^k$,
and the groupoid $\G_{\Phi,n}$ records this tame layer functorially through the collar groupoid $\G_C$.
Consequently, Kummer descent constraints for Stokes objects can be expressed as strict descent conditions
on the collar data (equivalently, as equivariant cocycle constraints on a finite skeleton).
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary} \label{cor:intro-van-kampen}
Let $X= X^{(1)}\cup X^{(2)}$ be an open cover compatible with $D$, and assume the sectorial/Stokes data are chosen compatibly on overlaps.
Then the presenting groupoids admit a pushout description reflecting this decomposition, so that questions about
$\Stokes_r(X^{\log}_n;D,\Phi)$ may be reduced to representations of an explicit groupoid obtained by gluing the local presenters.

\end{corollary}

For a fully explicit local model (including a finite Morita skeleton), the reader may jump directly to
\Cref{subsec:curve-model-clean}.
There we compute the presenting groupoid near a simple normal crossings corner and spell out the resulting
generators-and-relations (equivalently, nonabelian cocycle) description of the Stokes data.
This example is included as a concrete reference point: it displays, in a single diagram, the directional layer
($X^{\log}$), the tame/Kummer layer (the $(\mu_n)^k$-actions along strata), and the wild Stokes layer
(sector overlaps and Stokes jumps), and it provides a template for later computations.

After recalling the basic geometry of $X^{\log}_n$ in the SNC case and fixing conventions, we define the intrinsic groupoid
$\Stokes_r(X^{\log}_n;D,\Phi)$ and establish its torsor description.
We then construct the interior \v{C}ech groupoid $\G_U$, the collar \v{C}ech--Stokes groupoid $\G_C$, and the overlap groupoid $\G_{\times}$,
form the pushout \eqref{eq:pushout-intro}, and prove \Cref{thm:intro-main} in \Cref{sec:pushout}.
Finally, we discuss Morita invariance, Kummer descent along depth strata, and an explicit coequalizer
(generators-and-relations) model for $\G_{\Phi,n}$, including the SNC computation announced above.

For every $r\ge 1$, consider the $2$-fiber product of groupoids
\[
\Rep_r(\G_U)\times^{(2)}_{\Rep_r(\G_{\times})} \operatorname{Sec}(\pi).
\]
Which of the following groupoids is naturally equivalent to this $2$-fiber product, with the equivalence compatible with the restriction to $\Rep_r(\G_U)$ (forgetting the wild layer) and with the restriction to $\operatorname{Sec}(\pi)$ (forgetting the interior)?

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text: $\Stokes_r(X^{\log}_n;D,\Phi)$.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.text: The full subgroupoid of $\Stokes_r(X^{\log}_n;D,\Phi)$ consisting of objects whose wild/Stokes layer is trivial along $D$ (equivalently: the image of the restriction functor $\Stokes_r(X^{\log}_n;D,\Phi)\to\Rep_r(\G_U)$), with the evident compatibilities under forgetting the wild layer and forgetting the interior.

choices.label: D

choices.label: E

ALS.justification: The stem does not state or paraphrase the name of the correct groupoid, nor does it include a defining property that uniquely singles out choice A without doing the identification; the answer must be inferred from understanding the gluing/2-pullback description.

TAS.justification: For readers who have just seen the key result, the question is close to a recognition/recollection of a standard equivalence (“the 2-fiber product is the Stokes groupoid”). It’s not purely tautological because it asks for the *correct target groupoid* among several plausible but subtly different candidates, but it remains near-restatement-level.

GPS.justification: Choosing correctly requires generative reasoning about why the construction is a *2*-fiber product (vs strict), why \(\operatorname{Sec}(\pi)\) is the correct boundary/wild moduli rather than \(\Rep_r(\G_C)\), and why the outcome is the full Stokes groupoid rather than a trivial-wild sub-groupoid or the representation groupoid of a pushout presenter.

DQS.justification: Distractors are distinct and mathematically meaningful: (B) common 2-categorical vs 1-categorical pullback confusion, (C) plausible weaker/embedded subcase, (D) plausible but incorrect identification with representations of a glued/pushout groupoid, (E) plausible boundary-object misidentification. These align with realistic failure modes.

qa quality eval.overall_assessment: High-quality MCQ with no obvious answer leakage and strong, well-targeted distractors. It meaningfully tests understanding of 2-categorical gluing versus strict gluing and the role of the Stokes/wild layer, though it may function as near-theorem recall if the equivalence was stated immediately beforehand.

\label{main}
Let $H$ be a split classical group over $F$, 
and let $\phi \in \Phi_\mathrm{temp}(H(F))$. 
Suppose that one of the following holds: 
\begin{description}
\item[(B)]
$H = \SO_{2n+1}$, $p > 6n+3$ and $\phi$ is arbitrary; 
\item[(C)]
$H = \Sp_{2n}$, $p > 6n$ and $\phi$ satisfies $(\star)$; 
\item[(D)]
$H = \SO_{2n}$, $p > 6n$ and $\phi$ satisfies $(\star)$. 
\end{description}
Set $\psi = \widehat\phi$. 

\begin{enumerate}
\item
There exists $\pi \in \Pi_\psi$ such that 
\[
d_{H^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee)N_\phi) \in \bar\mathcal{N}(\pi)^{\max}.
\]
\item
For $\pi \in \Pi_\psi$ and for $\oo_H^\mathrm{st} \in \bar\mathcal{N}(\pi)$, 
if $\oo_H^\mathrm{st} \not= d_{H^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee)N_\phi)$, then 
\[
\dim(\oo_H^\mathrm{st}) < \dim(d_{H^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee)N_\phi)).
\]
Here, $\dim(\oo_H^\mathrm{st})$ is the Zariski dimension of the orbit as an algebraic variety.
\item
If we further assume Hypothesis \ref{hypo} below, then Conjecture \ref{upper} is true for $\phi$, i.e., 
\[
\bar\mathcal{N}(\pi)^{\max} \leq d_{H^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee)N_\phi)
\]
for any $\pi \in \Pi_\psi$.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{thm}\label{transfer}
Let $\oo_H^\st \in \NN(\h(\overline{F}))$ be a special nilpotent orbit.
Define $\oo_G^\st \in \NN(\g^\theta(\overline{F}))$ by 
\[
\oo_G^\st = d_{G^\vee}(\Ad(G^\vee)d_{H}(\oo_H^\st)).

post_theorem_intro_text:
\subsection{Outline of the proof}\label{sec.outline}
Throughout the paper, we assume that $p \gg 0$ as in Theorem \ref{main}.
The proof of Theorem \ref{main} is similar to the proofs of the Generic Packet Conjecture 
by Konno \cite{K} and Varma \cite{V}. 
The main idea is to compare local character expansions via 
\emph{endoscopic character identities}.
\par

Fix $\phi \in \Phi_\mathrm{temp}(H(F))$ and set $\psi = \widehat\phi$. 
Set $G = \GL_m$, where $m$ is the dimension of the standard representation $H^\vee \rightarrow G^\vee = \GL_m(\mathbb{C})$.
By composing with this map, we can regard $\psi$ as an $A$-parameter for $G(F)$, 
and obtain an irreducible self-dual representation $\pi_\psi$ of $G(F)$. 
Define an involution $\theta$ on $G(F)$ by 
\[
\theta(g) = J{}^tg^{-1}J^{-1}, 
\quad
J = \begin{pmatrix}
&&&1 \\
&&-1&\\
&\iddots&& \\
(-1)^{m-1}&&
\end{pmatrix} \in G(F).
\]
We can extend $\pi_\psi$ to an irreducible representation $\tl\pi_\psi$ of $G \rtimes \langle \theta \rangle$.
The twisted character of $\tl\pi_\psi$ is denoted by $\Theta_{\tl\pi_\psi}$. 
\par

Let $\Sc_\psi$ be the component group for $\psi$, 
and let $\widehat\Sc_\psi$ be its Pontryagin dual. 
Recall that Arthur defined a map
\[
\Pi_\psi \rightarrow \widehat\Sc_\psi, \;
\pi \mapsto \langle \cdot, \pi \rangle_\psi. 
\]
Notice that this is bijective since $\psi = \widehat\phi$.
Set $s_\psi = \psi(\1_{W_F}, \mathbf{1}, -\mathbf{1}) = \phi(\1_{W_F}, -\mathbf{1})$.
In this setting, \cite[Theorem 2.2.1]{Ar} asserts that 
\begin{description}
\item[(T1)]
the distribution
\[
S\Theta_{\psi} = \sum_{\pi \in \Pi_\psi} \langle s_\psi, \pi \rangle_\psi \Theta_\pi
\]
is stable, and $\Theta_{\tl\pi_\psi}$ is the transfer of $S\Theta_\psi$; 
\item[(T2)]
Each $s \in \Sc_\psi$ with $s \not= 1$ gives an elliptic endoscopic group $H_1 \times H_2$ of $H$
and an $A$-parameter $\psi_i$ for $H_i$ 
(of the form $\psi_i = \widehat\phi_i$ for some $\phi_i \in \Phi_\mathrm{temp}(H_i)$) such that 
\[
S\Theta_{\psi, s} = \sum_{\pi \in \Pi_\psi} \langle s \cdot s_\psi, \pi \rangle_\psi \Theta_\pi
\]
is the transfer of $S\Theta_{\psi_1} \otimes S\Theta_{\psi_2}$. 
\end{description}
\par

The first step of the proof of Theorem \ref{main} is to establish an analogue for the twisted $\GL_m$ case.
By the twisted local character expansion established by Clozel \cite[Theorem 3]{C}, 
we can expand
\[
\Theta_{\tl\pi_\psi} 
= \sum_{\oo_G \in \mathcal{N}(\mathfrak{g}^\theta(F))} c_{\oo_G}(\tl\pi_\psi) \hat\mu_{\oo_G}. 
\]
See Section \ref{sec.TLCE} below for the notations. 
We define $\NN_\theta(\tl\pi_\psi) \subset \mathcal{N}(\mathfrak{g}^\theta(F))$ 
and $\bar\NN_\theta(\tl\pi_\psi) \subset \mathcal{N}(\mathfrak{g}^\theta(\overline{F}))$
similar to $\mathcal{N}(\pi)$ and $\bar\mathcal{N}(\pi)$, respectively. 
In Theorem \ref{twist} below, we will show that 
\[
\bar\NN_\theta(\tl\pi_\psi)^{\max} = \{d_{G^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(G^\vee) N_\phi)\}.
\]
This is an immediate consequence of 
results of Konno \cite{K}, Varma \cite{V}, and M{\oe}glin--Waldspurger \cite{MW}.
Moreover, Konno's result \cite[Theorem 4.1(2)]{K} says that  
the constant $c_{\oo_G}(\tl\pi_\psi)$ for $\oo_G \subset d_{G^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(G^\vee) N_\phi)$ 
does not depend on the choice of the rational orbit.
\par

Set $\oo_H^\mathrm{st} = d_{H^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee) N_\phi)$ and $\oo_G^\mathrm{st} = d_{G^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(G^\vee) N_\phi)$.
The second step of the proof of Theorem \ref{main} is to show that 
there exists a constant $\gamma_{\oo_H}$ for each rational orbit $\oo_H \subset \oo_H^\mathrm{st}$ such that 
\[
\sum_{\oo_G \subset \oo_G^\mathrm{st}} \hat\mu_{\oo_G}
\quad
\text{is equal to the transfer of} 
\quad
\sum_{\oo_H \subset \oo_H^\mathrm{st}} \gamma_{\oo_H}\hat\mu_{\oo_H}
\]
on a small enough neighborhood of $\theta \in G(F) \rtimes \theta$.
See Theorem \ref{transfer} below. 
Hypothesis \ref{hypo} is an analogue of this result. 
These claims could be proven by similar arguments to the standard case explained in the next paragraph, 
but there is no explicit reference in the literature.
Thus we will prove Theorem \ref{transfer} in this paper. 
The proof uses Conjecture \ref{upper} in the case established in \cite{CMBO2},
which requires that $H$ is split over $F$.
\par

An analogous result for the standard endoscopy with unramified endoscopic groups
is known by Waldspurger \cite{W_pave}. 
Let $H_1 \times H_2$ be an unramified endoscopic group of $H$. 
For a special nilpotent orbit $\oo_{H_i}^\mathrm{st} \in \mathcal{N}(\h_i(\overline{F}))$, 
Waldspurger explicitly defined a nilpotent orbit
\[
\oo_H^\mathrm{st} = W(\oo_{H_1}^\mathrm{st}, \oo_{H_2}^\mathrm{st}) \in \mathcal{N}(\mathfrak{h}(\overline{F})),
\]
and proved a certain transfer result in \cite[XII.9 Th\'eor\`eme]{W_pave}.
The third step of the proof of Theorem \ref{main} is to relate the Waldspurger map $W(\oo_{H_1}^\mathrm{st}, \oo_{H_2}^\mathrm{st})$
and the Spaltenstein duality (Proposition \ref{WS}). 
\par

Combining the two transfer results, we can relate the local character expansion of $S\Theta_\psi$ (resp.~ $S\Theta_{\psi,s}$)
with the one of $\Theta_{\tl\pi_\psi}$ (resp.~ $S\Theta_{\psi_1} \otimes S\Theta_{\psi_2}$).
Then by induction on $m$, 
we can deduce Theorem \ref{main} in Section \ref{sec.proof}. 
To use \cite[XII.9 Th\'eor\`eme]{W_pave}, we need the condition ($\star$) in Cases (C) and (D), 
which is equivalent to saying that all endoscopic groups $H_1 \times H_2$ arising from $s \in \Sc_\psi$ are unramified. 

\begin{rem}\label{OvsSO}
The local Langlands correspondence for $H = \SO_{2n}$ as proven by Arthur, 
is given up to $\O_{2n}(F)$-conjugation. 
Thus, in turn, we should replace $\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee)N_\phi$ by $\mathrm{Ad}(\O_{2n}(\mathbb{C}))N_\phi$ in our results. 
We will ignore this discrepancy since it is not an important difference for the geometric wavefront set results.
By replacing $\SO_{2n}$ with $\O_{2n}$, we can use the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}
\item
the distributions on $\SO_{2n}(F)$ considered in the paper are all $\O_{2n}(F)$-invariant;
\item
the transfer of stable distributions on $H(F)$ to $G(F) \rtimes \theta$ is injective;
\item
$\mathrm{Ad}(G^\vee)\oo_{H^\vee} \cap H^\vee = \oo_{H^\vee}$ for $\oo_{H^\vee} \in \mathcal{N}(\mathfrak{h}^\vee)$.
\end{enumerate}
Note that (2) and (3) hold when $H = \SO_{2n+1}$ or $H = \Sp_{2n}$. 
\end{rem}

\[
S\Theta_{\psi}=\sum_{\pi\in\Pi_\psi}\langle s_\psi,\pi\rangle_\psi\,\Theta_\pi

\[

“is the transfer of $S\Theta_{\psi_1}\otimes S\Theta_{\psi_2}$.”

\begin{thm}\label{twist}
Let $\phi \colon W_F \times \SL_2(\C) \rightarrow G^\vee$ 
be a self-dual tempered $L$-parameter for $G(F) = \GL_m(F)$, 
and let $\pi_\psi$ be the Zelevinsky dual of the irreducible tempered representation 
$\pi_\phi$ corresponding to $\phi$. 
Then 
\[
\bar\NN_\theta(\tl\pi_\psi)^{\max} = \{d_{G^\vee}(\Ad(G^\vee) N_\phi)\}.
\]
Moreover, $c_{\oo_G}(\tl\pi_\psi) = c_{\oo_G'}(\tl\pi_\psi)$ 
for any rational orbits $\oo_G$ and $\oo_G'$ contained in $d_{G^\vee}(\Ad(G^\vee) N_\phi)$.
\end{thm}

This is described as “an immediate consequence of results of Konno \cite{K}, Varma \cite{V}, and M{\oe}glin--Waldspurger \cite{MW}.”

2) Writing $\oo_H^\mathrm{st}=d_{H^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee)N_\phi)$ and $\oo_G^\mathrm{st}=d_{G^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(G^\vee)N_\phi)$, “the second step” proves a transfer statement at the level of nilpotent orbital integrals, namely the following theorem.

\begin{thm}\label{transfer}
Let $\oo_H^\st \in \NN(\h(\overline{F}))$ be a special nilpotent orbit.
Define $\oo_G^\st \in \NN(\g^\theta(\overline{F}))$ by 
\[
\oo_G^\st = d_{G^\vee}(\Ad(G^\vee)d_{H}(\oo_H^\st)). 
\]
Then for each rational orbit $\oo_H \subset \oo_H^\st$, 
there exists a constant $\gamma_{\oo_H} \in \C$ such that 
\[
\sum_{\oo_G \subset \oo_G^\st} \hat\mu_{\oo_G}
\quad\text{is equal to the transfer of }\quad
\sum_{\oo_H \subset \oo_H^\st} \gamma_{\oo_H} \hat\mu_{\oo_H}
\]
on a small enough neighborhood of $\theta \in G(F) \rtimes \theta$.
\end{thm}

Hypothesis \ref{hypo} is described as an analogue of this result; explicitly:

\begin{hyp}\label{hypo}
Let $\oo_H^\st \in \NN(\h(\overline{F}))$ be a special nilpotent orbit.
Define $\oo_G^\st \in \NN(\g^\theta(\overline{F}))$ by 
\[
\oo_G^\st = d_{G^\vee}(\Ad(G^\vee)d_{H}(\oo_H^\st)). 
\]
Then for any constants $\{c_{\oo_H} \;|\; \oo_H \subset \oo_H^\st\}$ such that 
$\sum_{\oo_H \subset \oo_H^\st} c_{\oo_H} \hat\mu_{\oo_H}$ is stable, 
there exist constants $\{a_{\oo_G} \;|\; \oo_G \subset \oo_G^\st\}$ such that 
\[
\sum_{\oo_G \subset \oo_G^\st} a_{\oo_G} \hat\mu_{\oo_G}
\quad\text{is equal to the transfer of}\quad
\sum_{\oo_H \subset \oo_H^\st} c_{\oo_H} \hat\mu_{\oo_H} 
\]
on a small enough neighborhood of $\theta \in G(F) \rtimes \theta$.

\[
W(\oo_{H_1}^\st, \oo_{H_2}^\st) 
\leq d_{H^\vee}(\Ad(H^\vee)\xi(d_{H_1}(\oo_{H_1}^\st), d_{H_2}(\oo_{H_2}^\st))). 
\]

expanded_theorem:
\label{main}
Let $H$ be a split classical group over $F$, 
and let $\phi \in \Phi_\mathrm{temp}(H(F))$. 
Suppose that one of the following holds: 
\begin{description}
\item[(B)]
$H = \SO_{2n+1}$, $p > 6n+3$ and $\phi$ is arbitrary; 
\item[(C)]
$H = \Sp_{2n}$, $p > 6n$ and $\phi$ satisfies $(\star)$; 
\item[(D)]
$H = \SO_{2n}$, $p > 6n$ and $\phi$ satisfies $(\star)$. 
\end{description}
Set $\psi = \widehat\phi$. 

\begin{enumerate}
\item
There exists $\pi \in \Pi_\psi$ such that 
\[
d_{H^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee)N_\phi) \in \bar\mathcal{N}(\pi)^{\max}.
\]
\item
For $\pi \in \Pi_\psi$ and for $\oo_H^\mathrm{st} \in \bar\mathcal{N}(\pi)$, 
if $\oo_H^\mathrm{st} \not= d_{H^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee)N_\phi)$, then 
\[
\dim(\oo_H^\mathrm{st}) < \dim(d_{H^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee)N_\phi)).
\]
Here, $\dim(\oo_H^\mathrm{st})$ is the Zariski dimension of the orbit as an algebraic variety.
\item
If we further assume the following hypothesis, then the stated upper-bound conjecture holds for $\phi$.

\begin{hyp}\label{hypo}
Let $\oo_H^\st \in \NN(\h(\overline{F}))$ be a special nilpotent orbit.
Define $\oo_G^\st \in \NN(\g^\theta(\overline{F}))$ by 
\[
\oo_G^\st = d_{G^\vee}(\Ad(G^\vee)d_{H}(\oo_H^\st)). 
\]
Then for any constants $\{c_{\oo_H} \;|\; \oo_H \subset \oo_H^\st\}$ such that 
$\sum_{\oo_H \subset \oo_H^\st} c_{\oo_H} \hat\mu_{\oo_H}$ is stable, 
there exist constants $\{a_{\oo_G} \;|\; \oo_G \subset \oo_G^\st\}$ such that 
\[
\sum_{\oo_G \subset \oo_G^\st} a_{\oo_G} \hat\mu_{\oo_G}
\quad\text{is equal to the transfer of}\quad
\sum_{\oo_H \subset \oo_H^\st} c_{\oo_H} \hat\mu_{\oo_H} 
\]
on a small enough neighborhood of $\theta \in G(F) \rtimes \theta$.
\end{hyp}

We first record the conjecture in question.
\begin{conj}\label{upper}
Let $\phi \in \Phi(H(F))$. 
Then for any $\pi \in \Pi_\phi$, we have
\[
\bar\NN(\hat\pi)^{\max} \leq d_{H^\vee}(\Ad(H^\vee)N_\phi).
\]
Moreover, if $\phi$ is tempered, 
then the equality holds for some $\pi \in \Pi_\phi$. 
\end{conj}

In particular,
\[
\bar\mathcal{N}(\pi)^{\max} \leq d_{H^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee)N_\phi)
\]
for any $\pi \in \Pi_\psi$.
\end{enumerate}

correct_choice.label: A
correct_choice.text:
There exists $\pi\in\Pi_\psi$ such that
\[
 d_{H^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee)N_\phi)\in\bar{\mathcal N}(\pi)^{\max}.
\]
Moreover, for any $\pi\in\Pi_\psi$ and any $\oo_H^{\mathrm{st}}\in\bar{\mathcal N}(\pi)$, if $\oo_H^{\mathrm{st}}\neq d_{H^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee)N_\phi)$ then
\[
\dim(\oo_H^{\mathrm{st}})<\dim\bigl(d_{H^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee)N_\phi)\bigr),
\]
where $\dim(\oo_H^{\mathrm{st}})$ denotes the Zariski dimension of the orbit as an algebraic variety.

If, in addition, the following hypothesis holds: for every special nilpotent orbit $\oo_H^{\st}\in\NN(\h(\overline F))$, defining
\[
\oo_G^{\st}=d_{G^\vee}(\Ad(G^\vee)d_H(\oo_H^{\st}))\in\NN(\g^\theta(\overline F)),
\]
then for any constants $\{c_{\oo_H}\mid \oo_H\subset\oo_H^{\st}\}$ such that $\sum_{\oo_H\subset\oo_H^{\st}}c_{\oo_H}\,\hat\mu_{\oo_H}$ is stable, there exist constants $\{a_{\oo_G}\mid \oo_G\subset\oo_G^{\st}\}$ such that $\sum_{\oo_G\subset\oo_G^{\st}}a_{\oo_G}\,\hat\mu_{\oo_G}$ equals the transfer of $\sum_{\oo_H\subset\oo_H^{\st}}c_{\oo_H}\,\hat\mu_{\oo_H}$ on a sufficiently small neighborhood of $\theta\in G(F)\rtimes\theta$; under this hypothesis the upper-bound conjecture holds for $\phi$, namely: for any $\phi\in\Phi(H(F))$ and any $\pi\in\Pi_\phi$,
\[
\bar\NN(\hat\pi)^{\max}\le d_{H^\vee}(\Ad(H^\vee)N_\phi),
\]
and if $\phi$ is tempered then equality holds for some $\pi\in\Pi_\phi$. In particular,
\[
\bar{\mathcal N}(\pi)^{\max}\le d_{H^\vee}(\mathrm{Ad}(H^\vee)N_\phi)
\]
for every $\pi\in\Pi_\psi$.

choices.label: B
choices.text:
There exists $\pi\in\Pi_\psi$ such that
\[
 d_{H^\vee}(\Ad(H^\vee)N_\phi)\in\bar{\mathcal N}(\pi)^{\max}.
\]
Moreover, for any $\pi\in\Pi_\psi$ and any $\oo_H^{\mathrm{st}}\in\bar{\mathcal N}(\pi)$, if $\oo_H^{\mathrm{st}}\neq d_{H^\vee}(\Ad(H^\vee)N_\phi)$ then
\[
\dim(\oo_H^{\mathrm{st}})\le \dim\bigl(d_{H^\vee}(\Ad(H^\vee)N_\phi)\bigr).
\]
If, in addition, Hypothesis \textup{\ref{hypo}} holds, then the upper-bound conjecture holds for $\phi$ and the inequality
\[
\bar{\mathcal N}(\pi)^{\max}\le d_{H^\vee}(\Ad(H^\vee)N_\phi)
\]
holds for every $\pi\in\Pi_\psi$.

choices.label: C
choices.text:
Assume Hypothesis \textup{\ref{hypo}}. Then for every $\pi\in\Pi_\psi$ one has
\[
\bar{\mathcal N}(\pi)^{\max}\le d_{H^\vee}(\Ad(H^\vee)N_\phi).
\]
Moreover, there exists $\pi\in\Pi_\psi$ such that
\[
\dim\bigl(\oo_H^{\mathrm{st}}\bigr)\le \dim\bigl(d_{H^\vee}(\Ad(H^\vee)N_\phi)\bigr)
\quad\text{for all }\oo_H^{\mathrm{st}}\in\bar{\mathcal N}(\pi).
\]

choices.label: D
choices.text:
There exists $\pi\in\Pi_\psi$ such that
\[
 d_{H^\vee}(\Ad(H^\vee)N_\phi)\in\bar{\mathcal N}(\pi)^{\max}.
\]
Moreover, for any $\pi\in\Pi_\psi$ and any $\oo_H^{\mathrm{st}}\in\bar{\mathcal N}(\pi)$, if $\oo_H^{\mathrm{st}}\neq d_{H^\vee}(\Ad(H^\vee)N_\phi)$ then
\[
\dim(\oo_H^{\mathrm{st}})<\dim\bigl(d_{H^\vee}(\Ad(H^\vee)N_\phi)\bigr).
\]
If, in addition, the hypothesis of transfer in Hypothesis \textup{\ref{hypo}} holds for all (not necessarily special) nilpotent orbits $\oo_H^{\st}\in\NN(\h(\overline F))$, then the upper-bound conjecture holds for $\phi$ and, for any $\phi\in\Phi(H(F))$ and any $\pi\in\Pi_\phi$, one has
\[
\bar\NN(\hat\pi)^{\max}= d_{H^\vee}(\Ad(H^\vee)N_\phi)
\]
(with equality for every $\pi$ when $\phi$ is tempered).

choices.label: E
choices.text:
There exists $\pi\in\Pi_\psi$ such that
\[
 d_{H^\vee}(\Ad(H^\vee)N_\phi)\in\bar{\mathcal N}(\pi)^{\max}.
\]
Moreover, for any $\pi\in\Pi_\psi$ and any $\oo_H^{\mathrm{st}}\in\bar{\mathcal N}(\pi)$, if $\oo_H^{\mathrm{st}}\neq d_{H^\vee}(\Ad(H^\vee)N_\phi)$ then
\[
\dim(\oo_H^{\mathrm{st}})<\dim\bigl(d_{H^\vee}(\Ad(H^\vee)N_\phi)\bigr).
\]
If, in addition, the stated transfer hypothesis holds (for special $\oo_H^{\st}$), then the upper-bound conjecture holds for $\phi$ in the following strengthened form: for any $\phi\in\Phi(H(F))$ and any $\pi\in\Pi_\phi$,
\[
\bar\NN(\hat\pi)^{\max}\ge d_{H^\vee}(\Ad(H^\vee)N_\phi),
\]
and if $\phi$ is tempered, then equality holds for some $\pi\in\Pi_\phi$.

TAS.justification: The item is essentially a theorem/lemma identification task: it asks which option reproduces the exact existence/maximality/upper-bound conclusions under stated hypotheses, i.e., selecting the correct restatement rather than applying ideas to a new situation.

GPS.justification: Answering requires careful comparison of subtle logical/inequality differences (< vs ≤, special vs all orbits, ≤ vs ≥, equality-for-some vs equality-for-all), but it is mainly recognition/verification of the exact formal statement, not generative mathematical reasoning.

They are distinct and nontrivial.

theorem.content:
\label{thm:main}
Consider any $T \ge 1$ and $L,\alpha>0$. Then there exist an $\alpha$-strongly convex set $S$ and an $L$-smooth, $L$-strongly convex function $f$ in dimension $d=2(T+1)$ such that every \texttt{FO-LMO} method applied to $(f, S)$ with $x_0 = 0$ has $x_T$ infeasible or 
\[
f(x_T) - \min_{x\in S}f(x) \geq \frac{1}{528}\frac{L\, \mathrm{diam}(S)^2}{(T+1)^2}.
\]
Consequently, for any $\varepsilon>0$, there exist problem instances where $T\geq \sqrt{\frac{L\, \mathrm{diam}(S)^2}{528\varepsilon}} - 1$ iterations are required for any \texttt{FO-LMO} method to reach a suboptimality of $f(x_T) - \min_{x\in S}f(x) \leq \varepsilon$.
theorem.label: thm:main

post_theorem_intro_text:
While Theorem~\ref{thm:main} applies for any $L,\alpha>0$, it does not allow a free selection of $\mathrm{diam}(S)$. Rather, our constructed hard ``zero-chain'' set $S$ has $\mathrm{diam}(S) = \Theta(1/\alpha d)$. One cannot arbitrarily select $\alpha$ and $\mathrm{diam}(S)$ as they must satisfy, for example, that $\mathrm{diam}(S)\leq 2/\alpha$. In the limit where $\mathrm{diam}(S)= 2/\alpha$, the set $S$ is forced to be (up to translation) the ball $B(0,1/\alpha)$. Such forced structure enables faster algorithms\footnote{For example, when $\mathrm{diam}(S)= 2/\alpha$ and $S = B(0,1/\alpha)$, an LMO can be used to explicitly compute orthogonal projections onto the feasible region $S$. Then the class of \texttt{FO-LMO} methods includes projected gradient methods, which are known to converge linearly for smooth, strongly convex objectives.}. The development of hard instances for any selection of $\mathrm{diam}(S) \leq 2/\alpha$ and resulting more nuanced complexity bounds is left as an important future direction.

As a secondary result, we provide a partial generalization to $\beta$-smooth sets. These bounds are meaningful in the regime of only modestly smooth sets, having $\beta=\Omega(1/\sqrt{\varepsilon})$. In this regime, no \texttt{LMO-span} method (see Section~\ref{sec:SC} for a formal definition) can improve past the optimal compact convex set complexity of $\Theta(L\, \mathrm{diam}(S)^2/\varepsilon)$ or over the optimal $\alpha$-strongly convex set complexity of $\Theta(\sqrt{L\, \mathrm{diam}(S)^2/\varepsilon})$. Theorems~\ref{thm:smooth} and~\ref{thm:mixed} formalize these limits on acceleration due to smoothness.

Since our constructions throughout use an $L$-smooth, $L$-strongly convex objective, all of our lower bounds apply against the wider class of problems with smooth, strongly convex objectives having any $0 \leq \mu \leq L$. Hence, our theory highlights a fundamental difficulty of constrained optimization via LMOs: {\it Even on perfectly conditioned objective functions, hard adversarial constraint sets constitute a barrier to linear convergence.} This stands in contrast to gradient methods with an orthogonal projection oracle where convergence is dominated by objective function conditioning.

\paragraph{Outline.} Section~\ref{sec:SC} first derives a lower bound via a novel construction of a strongly convex feasible region that is hard for all \texttt{FO-LMO} methods with an additional span restriction. Section~\ref{sec:general} removes this restriction, proving Theorem~\ref{thm:main}. This construction is the main technical innovation of our work. Section~\ref{sec:smooth} then provides results extending lower bounds to the specialized setting of sets with modest levels of smoothness. 

\subsection{Related Work}
Our Theorem~\ref{thm:main} differs from the previously mentioned lower bounding result of~\cite{halbey2026lower} in two aspects, making the result complementary. In terms of algorithmic scope, our bound provides a wider guarantee, establishing a universal lower bound against all \texttt{FO-LMO} methods. In contrast,~\cite{halbey2026lower} provides a hard instance for two standard implementations of Frank-Wolfe, namely those fixing $p_k=\nabla f(x_k)$ and using an exact line search or the short stepsize procedure to select $x_{k+1}$. In terms of problem class scope, our construction requires a nonsmooth feasible region and a large problem dimension $d$ (linear in the number of iterations to be run). Such a high dimensionality assumption (i.e., $d>T$) is classical and widespread in the optimization complexity literature~\cite{nemirovski1983problem}. In contrast,~\cite{halbey2026lower} is able to provide a hard instance using a smooth ball in $d=2$ dimensions. As a result, they provide a stronger illustration of the limitations of the two methods that their theory covers.

As mentioned above, most classical lower bounding results in unconstrained first-order optimization rely on setting the problem dimension larger than the number of iterations to be conducted. This enables ``zero-chain'' arguments where the objective function is designed to reveal only one new coordinate to the given gradient-span algorithm at each iteration. The main technical innovation of our work is the design of a hard strongly convex set where the LMO possesses a similar zero-chain property to these classical hard objective constructions. Such constructions open the possibility to extend proof techniques and insights from existing unconstrained optimization lower bounds to constrained LMO/projection-free settings.

For example, although our strongly convex convergence rate lower bound matches the upper bound of~\cite{garber2015faster} in order, the two differ by constant factors: our lower bound has a universal constant of $1/528$ and their upper bound has $9/2$. This leaves open the question of determining exactly minimax optimal algorithms and hard problem instances. In settings of unconstrained first-order minimization, the Performance Estimation Problem (PEP) techniques pioneered by~\cite{drori2014performance,Interpolation,Interpolation2} have provided such theory. For example, in smooth convex optimization, these facilitated the identification of the Optimized Gradient Method~\cite{kim2016optimized} and an exactly matching lower bound~\cite{drori2017exact}. PEP was extended to cover structured smooth and strongly convex sets by Luner and Grimmer~\cite{luner2024performance}. As a result, future work may leverage PEP to similarly close the constant-factor gap left for \texttt{FO-LMO} methods.

Another important property of most Frank-Wolfe methods is that their trajectory is independent of the choice of inner product used. This differs from projected-gradient methods, where the choice of inner product and notion of orthogonality for projections affects the algorithm trajectory, making good preconditioning important for practical success. The line of work~\cite{Pena2023,Wirth2025,Wirth2026} provided Frank-Wolfe with ``affine-covariant'' convergence theory, matching the method's affine covariant nature by avoiding notions like smoothness and strong convexity defined in terms of a fixed inner product. Developing lower bounding theory in affine-covariant terms is an interesting future direction.

One can view the oracle model of an LMO as assuming first-order access to the support function $p \mapsto \sup\{\langle p, x\rangle \mid x\in S\}$. For sets with $0\in S$, a polar transformation establishes this as dual to assuming first-order access to the Minkowski gauge $y \mapsto \inf\{ \gamma>0 \mid y/\gamma \in S\}$. This gauge model has been studied by the works~\cite{Renegar2016,Grimmer2021-part1,Grimmer2021-part2,Zakaria2022,Lu2023} as an alternative projection-free framework. The works~\cite{liu2023gauges} and~\cite{samakhoana2024scalable} developed accelerated $\mathcal{O}(1/T^2)$ convergence guarantees for gauge methods over smooth sets, complementing the accelerated LMO rates for strongly convex sets. Identifying any structural relationships between the complexity of these dual oracle models and problem settings is another interesting direction.

Consider any $T \ge 1$ and $L,\alpha>0$. Then there exist an $\alpha$-strongly convex set $S$ and an $L$-smooth, $L$-strongly convex function $f$ in dimension $d=2(T+1)$ such that every \texttt{FO-LMO} method applied to $(f, S)$ with $x_0 = 0$ has $x_T$ infeasible or

sketch:
The post-theorem discussion explains (i) how earlier proofs of the lower bound worked in a special case, and (ii) why that approach fails for products of linear factors, motivating a different approach for Theorem~\ref{thm:asboundsPoly}.

- Prior method for the lower bound (used in \cite{KlurmanShkredovXu2023, ChinisShala2025} when $P$ has an irreducible factor of degree $\ge 2$): it uses that “there are many integers $n$ for which $P(n)$ has a prime factor greater than $n\log n$.”

- Example $P(n)=n^2+1$: for such $n$ one can “pull out” a unique large prime factor and still capture a “bulk” of the sum for infinitely many (sparse) $N$, via the heuristic decomposition
\[
\sum_{n\le N} f(n^2+1)\approx \sum_{N\log N < p\le N^2} f(p)\sum_{\substack{n\le N\\ p\mid n^2+1}} f\!\left(\frac{n^2+1}{p}\right).
\]

- After “conditioning on the small primes,” the right-hand side becomes “a weighted sum of independent random variables,” which is then treated “using intricate combinatorial arguments and Gaussian approximation.”

- Why this does not apply to Theorem~\ref{thm:asboundsPoly} for $P$ a product of linear factors: “for all its prime factors are of size at most linear in $N$,” so the large-prime-factor splitting is unavailable.

- Announced new approach (for Theorem~\ref{thm:asboundsPoly}): “a different method that does not involve any combinatorial splitting of the sum or conditioning,” instead to “fully utilize the martingale structure of the entire sum.” (Details are deferred: “we will elaborate on this in the next section.”)

mcq.question: Let $f$ be a Rademacher or Steinhaus random multiplicative function. In the Rademacher case, assume $P\in\mathbb Z[x]$ is either (i) a product of at least two distinct linear factors over $\mathbb Q$, or (ii) an irreducible polynomial of degree $2$ taking infinitely many square-free values. In the Steinhaus case, assume $P(x)$ is not of the form $w(x+c)^d$ for $w\in\mathbb Z$ and $c\in\mathbb Q$. Which statement asserts the almost sure existence of asymptotic bounds for the partial sums $\sum_{n\le N} f(P(n))$, including an almost sure subsequence along which the bound is attained up to constants?
